identityReview: Helen Elizabeth Clark, born 26 February 1950 in Hamilton and raised in Te Pahu. New Zealand’s second woman prime minister, serving 10 December 1999–19 November 2008, and first woman to lead UNDP, April 2009–April 2017. Current Gavi Board chair from January 2026, distinct from CEO Sania Nishtar. Preserve the 1996–1999 Owairaka constituency interval, 1993 Labour leadership and honorary nature of the 2010 LLD. Chatham House’s 2021 election is recorded historically without inferring either a current presidency or a resignation from an inconsistent current roster.
lifeStatusEvidence: AAP’s 8 November 2026 interview, read on 1News, directly quotes Clark about electoral-law review and establishes recent activity. Gavi’s board roster updated 5 November 2026 independently confirms her current board-chair role; the July meeting release also quotes her in that role. These textual records do not claim a visual attendance check or turn her electoral criticism into a legal finding.

sourceReview.accessMethod: Read Parliament’s archived biography, personal-biography childhood/career passages, Auckland’s alumni paragraph, NZ History biography and Treaty-law section, UNDP’s Clark section, WHO’s appointment release, selected pandemic-panel presentation passages, Chatham House’s 2021 announcement, AAP interview passages, Gavi appointment/profile/board table and selected July meeting sections. Statutory repeal status was available in official indexed text while the body returned 403. Read Commons crop/parent metadata and public VRT/licence notices, not private permission correspondence or image pixels.
corrections: Read the New Zealand Parliament archived biography. It gives 26 February 1950 in Hamilton, ministerial dates, 8 August 1989–2 November 1990 as deputy prime minister, and 10 December 1999–19 November 2008 as prime minister. Its constituency record distinguishes Mount Albert before/after Owairaka in 1996–1999; do not repeat simplified claims of one unchanged constituency throughout 1981–2009. The party-activities section lists a 1996 Labour-leader start inconsistent with its own 1 December 1993 opposition-leader record and official NZ History; use corroborated 1993, not the isolated 1996 entry. It lists final parliamentary service through 18 April 2009 while raw summaries use 17 April; the dossier uses April only.

Read the personal biography’s childhood and early-career sections. It distinguishes Hamilton hospital birthplace from the Te Pahu farm where she grew up; 1968 is enrolment, not graduation. It corroborates study/teaching, 1987–1990 ministerial experience, 1989–1990 deputy premiership and 1993 party leadership. Its uninterrupted Mount Albert shorthand is refined by Parliament’s constituency record. Promotional economic assessments are not treated as independently measured personal achievements or proof that policy was uncontested.

Read the alumni paragraph of the University of Auckland 2015–2016 Profile. It explicitly records BA 1971, MA 1974 and LLD (Honorary) 2010. The honorary law degree is not an earned research doctorate, and its then-current UNDP description is historical. No claim is made to have audited academic transcripts or the entire PDF. The file’s later indexing/upload date is not the degree or publication period.

Read the NZ History biography passages. They distinguish Jenny Shipley as the first woman prime minister from Clark as the first woman to take office following an election victory, and corroborate the three consecutive Labour election victories and 1993 leadership transition. A prime minister is not directly elected in a separate nationwide presidential-style election. The source describes policy moderation rather than wholesale reversal of Rogernomics, union/civil-rights reforms and a new Supreme Court. The dossier does not assign every economic outcome to Clark alone.

Read the Helen Clark section of UNDP’s past-administrators page. It explicitly gives April 2009–April 2017 and first female administrator, with concurrent chairmanship of the UN Development Group. Her UNDP role is neither secretary-general nor a current 2026 appointment. Other administrators’ biographies on the same page, especially their education and awards, were not transferred to her. No unsupported exact April start/end day or independent transparency-ranking result is added.

Read WHO’s 9 July 2020 announcement of the independent evaluation. Clark and Ellen Johnson Sirleaf are co-chairs, selected following consultation and a World Health Assembly mandate; they choose the other members and secretariat. This is an independent evaluation, not appointment as WHO director-general. The Nobel Peace Prize reference belongs to Sirleaf, not Clark. The announcement’s future reporting timetable is not itself proof the eventual report was delivered; the May 2021 presentation separately establishes that event.

Read the panel’s presentation header, selected findings and recommendation passages, including the named speakers. The presentation occurred on 12 May 2021, while the web page is dated 19 May. It summarises assessment of early warning/response and calls for stronger WHO authority, financing, vaccine equity and preparedness. Recommendations are collective proposals, not proof of a new binding treaty or full implementation. Sirleaf’s passages are not automatically Clark’s personal quotations. No claim to have reviewed the complete main report, all evidence annexes or video recording is made; historical casualty/dose figures and proposed financing amounts were not carried forward as current totals.

Read Chatham House’s 23 July 2021 election announcement, updated 17 August. It names Clark as replacing John Major and joining two other serving presidents; that is institute governance rather than director/CEO or sole president. It independently identifies her as the eighth UNDP administrator and first woman. The timeline dates the announcement, not an independently verified installation ceremony. Current Chatham presidency is not asserted as the dossier’s main 2026 office because the latest role-filtered roster omits her despite 2025 and July 2026 materials naming her.

Read the official Treaty timeline’s 2004 section. It records passage of the Foreshore and Seabed Act in November, Crown ownership/public-access provisions, widespread Māori opposition regarding customary rights and Treaty obligations, the May hīkoi and formation of the Māori Party. The public text attributes the rights/Treaty criticism to Māori opponents; it is not a claimed judicial conviction of Clark or a declaration that the law remains in force. No original tribunal report or full contemporaneous legislative debate was reviewed.

Read the official New Zealand Legislation indexed status text: the 2004 Act was repealed on 1 April 2011 by section 5 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011. Opening the full statute returned HTTP 403. The repeal status is used narrowly, not to claim review of the full legal text, all later amendments or current individual customary-title litigation.

Read the AAP-bylined 1News report at its 8 November 2026 URL, especially the direct-interview passage. Clark calls for review of electoral, enrolment and campaign-funding rules; this is recent interview evidence. Her view that the election might be flawed is not a final judicial or observer ruling. The report describes preliminary results and additional ballots due on 27 November, which remains future at this cutoff; no final seat count, coalition outcome or invalidation is asserted. No linked video or social-media account was independently examined.

Read Gavi’s 6 October 2025 appointment release. It distinguishes selection in October 2025 from the January 2026 start, succession to José Manuel Barroso and Sania Nishtar’s separate CEO position. The announcement alone would be prospective; current board membership and the January biography establish the role was taken up. Its description of future strategic priorities and funding ambitions is not a verified record of already delivered benefits.

Read Gavi’s board-members table, explicitly updated 5 November 2026. It lists Helen Clark in the independent individual/chair seat, with term scheduled to end 31 December 2027, and Sania Nishtar as CEO. The board roster supports the current chairmanship; a scheduled term end is not a guarantee of future service. It is a governance record rather than independent proof of a particular in-person appearance.

Read Gavi’s Helen Clark board-chair biography, updated 6 January 2026. It confirms January commencement and April 2009–April 2017 UNDP service. Its list of other boards and rankings was not adopted wholesale as independently refreshed current facts. Honorary or advocacy positions are not conflated with executive management; no claim is made that UNDP’s performance was caused by one person alone.

Read selected sections of Gavi’s 2 July 2026 board-meeting release. It identifies Clark as chair and Nishtar as CEO, differentiates decisions for 2026–2030 from the previous 2021–2025 period, and notes financing constraints and targets. Target vaccinations, mortality reduction, economic benefits and approved financing access are not already delivered outcomes or disbursed funds. Earlier-period achievements are not assigned to Clark’s chairmanship beginning in 2026. Future effective dates for other board appointments were not confused with the announcement date.

additionalConsulted.access: Read the parliamentary firsts table, corroborating Clark’s 8 August 1989 deputy premiership and 1 December 1993 opposition leadership, Shipley’s 1997 premiership and Clark’s 1999 election-related first. The wording does not establish direct popular election of the prime minister.

Read the 3 September 2025 announcement: May and Amos approved on 2 September, with different start dates; Clark remains named in the then-planned lineup. Bronwen Maddox is director/CEO. This is historical corroboration, not sufficient by itself to settle the November 2026 roster discrepancy.

Read the current role-filtered listing. It names Amos, May and president emeritus Major, but does not show Clark. Search had an older indexed Clark entry. Absence alone does not establish resignation or an end date, so no invented transition is supplied.

Read indexed conference programme passages naming Clark on the presidents panel. The event page was opened, but not every programme or recording was examined. A programme listing is not by itself proof of attendance or her November office status.
Read parent metadata, CC BY-SA 4.0 conditions, upload history and the public VRT permission notice. Did not access the restricted ticket correspondence or review photo pixels.

sourceReview.limits: AI editorial and translation review, not certified native-language human review. No degree transcript, complete statutory text or tribunal file, complete pandemic evidence archive, election recount or ruling, private permission correspondence, recordings or portrait pixels were reviewed. Resolve the Chatham House roster discrepancy before asserting a current role. Refresh current offices, electoral developments and policy outcomes before publication; forecasts, targets, critique and proposals are not completed results or court findings.

translationReview.scope: All 32 display fields in seven foreign languages reviewed against Chinese and English. Preserve Hamilton birthplace versus Te Pahu upbringing; BA/MA versus honorary LLD; Mount Albert/Owairaka constituency interval; 1993 leadership versus the conflicting 1996 archived line; second woman PM versus first woman after an election victory; 1989 deputy role; historical UNDP role versus UN secretary-general; joint pandemic evaluation and recommendation/implementation distinction; historical three-person Chatham presidency versus CEO; 2025 appointment versus 2026 Gavi start and Sania Nishtar’s separate CEO role; Māori criticism and 2011 repeal; attributed 2026 electoral comments versus invalidation.
